questions.question: Explain why 'the economy grew' and 'the average South African got poorer' can both be true in the same year, using the two measurement corrections from the lesson.
questions.expected_answer: Growth must be measured in real terms (constant prices, stripping out inflation) and then per capita (divided by population). Total real GDP can grow — say around 1% a year — while population grows faster (about 1,5%), so real GDP per capita falls: the pot is bigger but the plates are smaller. Nominal figures can also exaggerate growth when inflation is high, so both corrections — real, then per person — are needed before judging living standards.

questions.question: Describe the Lorenz curve diagram fully in words — axes, diagonal, curve — and define the Gini coefficient with its endpoints and South Africa's value.
questions.expected_answer: Horizontal axis: cumulative percentage of the population from poorest to richest; vertical axis: cumulative percentage of income. The straight diagonal from bottom-left to top-right is the line of perfect equality — any share of people holds that same share of income. The actual Lorenz curve runs corner to corner but sags below the diagonal (in SA the poorest 60% receive only about 10% of income); the deeper the sag, the greater the inequality. The Gini coefficient is the area between diagonal and curve divided by the whole area under the diagonal: 0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person holds everything. South Africa's is about 0,63 — the highest of any major economy.

questions.question: Name the four kinds of redistribution methods used in South Africa with an example of each, and state the growth-redistribution tension in both directions.
questions.expected_answer: Progressive taxation (income tax brackets up to 45%, VAT zero-rating staples to soften regressivity); cash transfers (about 28 million social grants — old-age, child support, disability, SRD); redistribution in kind (free basic water and electricity, no-fee schools, feeding schemes, RDP housing, clinics); labour-market and asset measures (minimum wage, B-BBEE, land reform, and education spending that redistributes future earning power). Tension: redistribution is funded from growth, and over-taxing can drive away investment; but extreme inequality itself brakes growth, since people without food, skills or transport cannot produce or buy. Done well, growth and redistribution are complements — each feeds the other.
